reorder-point.formula: z = inverse_normal(service_level / 100); safety_stock = z x demand_sd x sqrt(lead_time_days); reorder_point = avg_daily_demand x lead_time_days + safety_stock.
reorder-point.edition: Reorder point and safety stock (standard service-level inventory control), first-principles, by name; the actual demand pattern and supplier reliability govern.
reorder-point.freeAccess: The service-level reorder-point and safety-stock relations are standard published inventory-management results; the demand, lead time, and variability come from the business's records.
reorder-point.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
reorder-point.editionNote: Reorder point and safety stock (service-level model). z = the inverse-normal of the service level (95% = 1.645, 99% = 2.326), safety_stock = z x demand_sd x sqrt(lead_time), and reorder_point = avg_daily_demand x lead_time + safety_stock. The buffer scales with the SQUARE ROOT of the lead time and with the z-score, so chasing the last few points of service costs a disproportionate buffer -- moving from 95% to 99% raises the safety stock by about 40% (z 1.645 to 2.326) for a 4-point gain. The model assumes normally distributed demand and a fixed lead time; variable lead time adds a second variance term. A planning aid, not an inventory policy; the actual demand pattern and supplier reliability govern.

assumptions.name: Two parts
assumptions.value: reorder point = demand during lead time + a safety-stock buffer

assumptions.name: Square-root scaling
assumptions.value: safety stock scales with sqrt(lead time) and the z-score; the last points cost a disproportionate buffer

assumptions.name: Fixed lead time
assumptions.value: assumes normal demand and a fixed lead time; variable lead time adds a second variance term

voltage-drop.formula: VD = 2 x K x I x L / cmil single-phase; sqrt(3) replaces 2 for three-phase; K = 12.9 (Cu) / 21.2 (Al) ohm-cmil/ft, the 75 C stranded basis of NEC Chapter 9 Table 8. DC resistance only: no reactance, no power factor (use voltage-drop-reactance for that).
voltage-drop.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Chapter 9 Tables 8 and 9; IEEE 141 by name.
voltage-drop.freeAccess: Free read-only access at nfpa.org/freeaccess. IEEE 141 is licensed; principles free at university OCW and IEEE-USA outreach.
voltage-drop.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
voltage-drop.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Conductor temperature
assumptions.value: 75°C (fixed in K)

assumptions.name: Power factor
assumptions.value: not modeled; resistive drop only
assumptions.source: engineering practice for general lighting / receptacle loads

assumptions.name: Voltage-drop target
assumptions.value: 3% branch + 5% feeder = 5% total

service-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.

assumptions.name: Voltage
assumptions.value: 240 V single-phase split for dwelling unless user supplies

assumptions.name: Demand factor for first 3 kVA general lighting
assumptions.value: 100% (per NEC 2023 Table 220.45)

vbelt-drive.formula: ratio = driver_rpm / driven_rpm = D_driven / D_driver; belt length L = 2C + (pi/2)(D1+D2) + (D2-D1)^2/(4C); design_HP = nameplate_HP * service_factor; belts = ceil(design_HP / HP_per_belt).
vbelt-drive.edition: ANSI/RMA IP-20 (Classical V-belts); ANSI/RMA IP-22 (Narrow V-belts). Gates Industrial Drive Design Manual (public).
vbelt-drive.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
vbelt-drive.editionNote: HP-per-belt is a coarse planning default by cross-section; the manufacturer's speed-specific table governs.

assumptions.name: HP per belt
assumptions.value: coarse nominal by cross-section (A 3 / B 7 / C 15 / D 30 / 3V 5 / 5V 12 / 8V 30 HP); verify against the manufacturer power table

assumptions.name: Driver pitch diameter
assumptions.value: entered by the user; the driven diameter follows from the ratio

cattle-heart-girth-weight.formula: live_weight_lb = heart_girth_in^2 x body_length_in / 300 (Schaeffer's formula). Heart girth = circumference behind the front legs; body length = point of shoulder to pin bone; both in inches.
cattle-heart-girth-weight.edition: Cattle live-weight estimation from heart girth (Schaeffer's formula; Penn State / University of Missouri Extension 'Estimating Cattle Weight'), by name; a certified scale governs a sale weight and a vet or the weigh-tape maker's chart governs a dose.
cattle-heart-girth-weight.freeAccess: The heart-girth weight relation is public extension-service practice; the girth and length are the animal's tape measurements.
cattle-heart-girth-weight.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cattle-heart-girth-weight.editionNote: When a producer needs a beef animal's weight and no scale is available, a cloth tape and Schaeffer's formula give a usable estimate. Two measurements are taken in inches: the heart girth, the circumference of the body just behind the front legs where the tape crosses the barrel at the level of the heart, and the body length, the straight-line distance from the point of the shoulder back to the pin bone at the point of the rump. The estimated live weight in pounds is the heart girth squared, times the body length, divided by 300. A steer measuring 70 inches around the heart girth and 55 inches long estimates 70 times 70 times 55 divided by 300, or about 898 pounds; a smaller animal at 60 by 48 inches estimates 576 pounds. The heart girth is squared because it stands in for the cross-sectional area of the barrel, which is the biggest driver of body mass, so a repeatable reading depends on pulling the tape snug at the smallest point right behind the shoulder with the animal standing squarely on level ground. The formula is calibrated for mature beef-type cattle and is least accurate for very young calves, very fat or very thin animals, dairy-type conformation, and heavily pregnant cows; commercial weigh tapes printed for cattle fold the length term into a girth-only scale and make the same kind of estimate. This is an on-farm working estimate; a certified livestock scale governs an actual sale weight, and a veterinarian or the tape manufacturer's chart governs a medication dose or a marketing decision.

assumptions.name: Schaeffer's formula
assumptions.value: weight (lb) = heart girth^2 x body length / 300, both in inches; girth behind front legs, length shoulder-point to pin bone
assumptions.source: Penn State / Univ. of Missouri Extension

assumptions.name: Calibration range
assumptions.value: for mature beef-type cattle; off for very young/fat/thin, dairy-type, or heavily pregnant animals; a certified scale governs a sale weight

header-sizing.formula: Tributary uniform load w (plf) = total area load (psf) × supported width (ft); roof = the greater of ground snow and the 20 psf roof live load, + 15 psf dead, each floor adds 50 psf. Smallest built-up member with min(L_bending, L_deflection) ≥ span, where Fb is adjusted by load-duration C_D and size factor C_F. Jack studs each end = ceil(end reaction / (F_c-perp × 5.25 in²)).
header-sizing.edition: IRC 2021 (International Residential Code). §R602.7 (headers). AWC NDS-2018 (National Design Specification for Wood Construction). reference design values, load-duration C_D and size factor C_F.
header-sizing.freeAccess: Free read-only access at codes.iccsafe.org. AWC NDS free at awc.org.
header-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
header-sizing.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow IRC 2021. Jurisdictions on IRC 2018 / 2024 differ at the margins; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Load assembly
assumptions.value: roof = max(ground snow, 20 psf roof live) + 15 psf dead; each floor above = 40 psf live + 10 psf dead

assumptions.name: Load-duration factor C_D
assumptions.value: 1.15 snow (roof-only) / 1.0 occupancy (floors above)

assumptions.name: Cross-check
assumptions.value: allowable spans verified against IRC Table R602.7(1) by physics; discrepancies flagged

containment-air-balance.formula: Orifice flow Q = 2610 × A × sqrt(ΔP) (cfm; A in ft², ΔP in inches WC). Leakage area is entered in in² and converted to ft² (/144). Recommended NAM count = required_negative_flow / per-NAM rated CFM.
containment-air-balance.edition: Classical orifice-flow theory; constant 2610 from ASHRAE Fundamentals derivation. IICRC S520-2024 §12 for containment guidance.
containment-air-balance.freeAccess: Orifice-flow derivations free in published engineering texts.
containment-air-balance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Orifice constant 2610
assumptions.value: from ASHRAE Fundamentals (sharp-edge orifice, dry air, sea level)

assumptions.name: Default ΔP target
assumptions.value: 0.02 in WC (negative pressure inside containment)

extinguisher-coverage.formula: grid spacing = travel distance x sqrt(2); area per extinguisher = 2 x travel^2 (the worst-case point on a square grid sits at the centre of a square, sqrt(2)/2 of the spacing away); count by travel = ceil(floor area / area per extinguisher); count by the area ceiling = ceil(floor area / cap); required = the larger of the two.
extinguisher-coverage.edition: NFPA 10 - a maximum travel distance to a Class A extinguisher of 75 ft at all hazard levels, 30 ft for Class K, and 30 or 50 ft for Class B depending on the extinguisher's B rating and the hazard level; and the 6.1.3.3 ceiling of 11,250 sq ft of coverage per extinguisher. The square-grid relation is geometry, not a code value.
extinguisher-coverage.freeAccess: The travel distances and the area ceiling are widely quoted figures. NFPA 10's maximum-area-per-unit-of-A table by hazard classification is NOT reproduced, and Class D travel distances are not shipped.
extinguisher-coverage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
extinguisher-coverage.editionNote: The finding worth the tile is that NFPA 10's two Class A limits are the same limit wearing different clothes. On an idealised clear floor with extinguishers on a square grid, the farthest anyone stands from one is the centre of a square, which is sqrt(2)/2 of the grid spacing - so the spacing can be the travel distance times sqrt(2) and each unit covers 2 x travel^2. At 75 ft that is 11,250 sq ft exactly, which is the 6.1.3.3 ceiling. The area cap is not an independent safety margin; it is the geometry of the travel distance, and knowing that tells you the ceiling ALREADY assumes a perfectly open floor with nothing in the way. Which leads to the caveat that outranks all of the arithmetic: travel distance is measured along the PATH OF TRAVEL, not in a straight line. A 75 ft walk around a partition can be 40 ft as the crow flies, so a warehouse with racking or an office with corridors will need more units than any area calculation suggests. The tile says explicitly that its count is a FLOOR and that the number only goes up once the routes are walked. Class K makes the point from the other direction: at 30 ft a unit covers only 1,800 sq ft, so travel distance governs by a wide margin and an area-based count would be badly wrong. What the tile does NOT determine is the extinguisher RATING. NFPA 10 separately sets a maximum floor area per unit of A by hazard classification - light, ordinary, and extra each differ - and that table decides whether a 2-A, a 4-A, or something larger is needed. It is not reproduced here, and a floor with the right NUMBER of extinguishers at too small a rating still fails. Class B travel distance is entered rather than assumed because it depends on the B rating and hazard level together. Class D is deliberately absent. Also not checked: mounting height and the weight thresholds that change it, visibility and signage, obstruction of the unit itself, inspection and maintenance intervals, and whether the occupancy requires extinguishers at all. A planning aid, not a fire-protection design; NFPA 10 as adopted, the fire code official, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Class A travel
assumptions.value: 75 ft at all hazard levels

assumptions.name: Class K travel
assumptions.value: 30 ft to a wet-chemical unit, in addition to the room's Class A coverage

assumptions.name: Class B travel
assumptions.value: 30 or 50 ft by B rating and hazard level - entered, not assumed

assumptions.name: Area ceiling
assumptions.value: 11,250 sq ft per extinguisher, which equals 2 x 75^2

assumptions.name: Path of travel
assumptions.value: measured along the walking route, so the grid count is an open-floor FLOOR

assumptions.name: Rating not determined
assumptions.value: the maximum-area-per-unit-of-A table by hazard class is separate and not reproduced

relay-pump-distance.formula: budget = max_discharge - intake_residual - 0.434 x elevation; FL_per_100 = C x (target_flow / 100)^2; max_distance = budget / FL_per_100 x 100.
relay-pump-distance.edition: IFSTA Pumping Apparatus Driver/Operator relay pumping maximum distance, by name.
relay-pump-distance.freeAccess: The relay-pumping relations are public fire-service training material; the SOP and the pump's real capability govern the actual relay.
relay-pump-distance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
relay-pump-distance.editionNote: The next pumper needs a 20 psi residual on its intake or it cavitates, so the usable pressure is the max discharge minus 20 minus the lift - not the whole pump; the distance falls with the square of flow (doubling gpm quarters the spacing, why big water uses large-diameter hose and more pumpers, not more pressure); the elevation term is 0.434 psi per foot; the SOP and the pump's real capability govern - a planning aid, not incident command.

assumptions.name: Intake residual
assumptions.value: hold 20 psi at the next intake so the pump does not cavitate

assumptions.name: Square-law spacing
assumptions.value: FL per 100 ft scales with (Q/100)^2, so doubling the flow quarters the distance

handrail-geometry.formula: height 34 in to 38 in to the top of the gripping surface, measured above walking surfaces, stair nosings, and ramp surfaces. Clearance behind the grip 1-1/2 in minimum. Circular grip 1-1/4 in to 2 in outside diameter; non-circular grip perimeter 4 in to 6-1/4 in AND cross-section dimension 2-1/4 in maximum. Extensions: 12 in horizontal at the top of a stair and at both ends of a ramp; at the bottom of a stair, one TREAD DEPTH of horizontal distance at the slope of the flight.
handrail-geometry.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 505.4, 505.5, 505.7.1, 505.7.2, 505.10.1, 505.10.2, and 505.10.3. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
handrail-geometry.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
handrail-geometry.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
handrail-geometry.editionNote: The height is the part everybody knows and still gets half wrong, because 34 to 38 in is a RANGE - a handrail can be too high, which surprises people who treat 34 as the only number. It is measured to the top of the GRIPPING SURFACE, vertically above walking surfaces, stair NOSINGS, and ramp surfaces, so on a stair the measurement runs from the nosing line rather than from the tread. Three requirements get missed. The clearance behind the grip is 1-1/2 in minimum between the gripping surface and any adjacent surface, and it is the one a wall-mounted bracket eats without anyone noticing, because the rail looks clear until a hand wraps it. The grip itself is a WINDOW in both directions: a circular rail is 1-1/4 in minimum to 2 in maximum in outside diameter, so a 2-1/2 in rail is not a generous handrail but a noncompliant one, too fat to grip and failing as surely as a thin one. A non-circular rail carries two conditions rather than one - a perimeter of 4 in to 6-1/4 in AND a cross-section dimension of 2-1/4 in maximum - so a wide flat rail can meet the perimeter and fail the cross section. And the extensions are ASYMMETRIC, which is the part that gets built wrong. At the top of a stair the rail extends 12 in horizontally beginning directly above the first riser nosing. At the BOTTOM it extends at the SLOPE OF THE FLIGHT for a horizontal distance at least equal to one TREAD DEPTH beyond the last riser nosing - so the bottom extension is a function of the stair rather than a fixed number, and on a 13 in tread the 12 in people assume is an inch short while on an 11 in tread it is an inch wasted. At a ramp both ends take a flat 12 in horizontal and the sloped rule does not apply. Not checked: continuity, which 505.6 requires along the tops and sides of the gripping surface without obstruction; whether handrails are required on this run at all and on how many sides; the 505.10 exceptions, including those for aisle handrails and for extensions that would be hazardous or intrude into a circulation path; the rail's structural capacity, which is a code load case rather than a dimension; the stair or ramp itself - riser, tread, nosing profile, slope, landings, and cross slope; guards, which are a different element with different heights; and state and local accessibility law and the building code. A handrail dimension screen, not a stair design.

assumptions.name: Height
assumptions.value: 34 in minimum to 38 in maximum, to the top of the gripping surface above nosings

assumptions.name: Clearance
assumptions.value: 1-1/2 in minimum between the gripping surface and adjacent surfaces

assumptions.name: Circular grip
assumptions.value: 1-1/4 in minimum to 2 in maximum outside diameter

assumptions.name: Non-circular grip
assumptions.value: perimeter 4 in to 6-1/4 in, and cross-section dimension 2-1/4 in maximum

assumptions.name: Top extension at stairs
assumptions.value: 12 in horizontal beginning directly above the first riser nosing

assumptions.name: Bottom extension at stairs
assumptions.value: one tread depth of horizontal distance, at the slope of the flight

assumptions.name: Ramp extensions
assumptions.value: 12 in horizontal above the landing at both ends

metal-weight.formula: weight = cross-sectional area * length * density * quantity. Per-shape area from geometry: tube = pi/4 * (OD^2 - ID^2), hex = 0.866 * width^2, round = pi/4 * dia^2, etc. lb to kg via x 0.453592.
metal-weight.edition: First-principles weight = volume x density. Densities are the published nominal values for the common alloys (carbon steel 0.2836, stainless 0.289, aluminum 6061 0.098, copper 0.323, brass 0.307 lb/in^3) or user-supplied.
metal-weight.freeAccess: The density values are published nominal references; mill certs and the actual alloy temper govern the real figure.
metal-weight.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
metal-weight.editionNote: Single-edition (geometry plus nominal alloy densities). Nominal pipe-size differs from actual OD; enter the actual OD/ID.

assumptions.name: Alloy density
assumptions.value: published nominal lb/in^3 by alloy, or user-supplied

grinding-wheel-rpm.formula: SFPM = pi x wheel_diameter_in x RPM / 12; max_rpm = rated_max_sfpm x 12 / (pi x wheel_diameter_in); actual_sfpm = pi x wheel_diameter_in x grinder_rpm / 12; within rating when grinder_rpm <= max_rpm.
grinding-wheel-rpm.edition: Surface-speed identity, first-principles; the wheel's rated maximum operating speed (SFPM) comes from the wheel blotter and the machine speed from the nameplate. Per ANSI B7.1.
grinding-wheel-rpm.freeAccess: The surface-speed relation is a first-principles geometric identity (circumference x rev/min); the wheel's rated SFPM and the grinder RPM are read from the wheel blotter and the machine nameplate.
grinding-wheel-rpm.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
grinding-wheel-rpm.editionNote: A grinding wheel is rated for a maximum operating SPEED in surface feet per minute (SFPM), printed on its paper blotter. Surface speed is SFPM = pi x D(in) x RPM / 12, so a given wheel diameter has a maximum RPM = rated SFPM x 12 / (pi x D). NEVER mount a wheel on a machine whose spindle speed exceeds the wheel's rating -- an over-speed wheel can burst. As the wheel wears smaller its safe RPM rises, but the machine speed is fixed, so a fresh (larger) wheel is the governing case. Per ANSI B7.1 (safety requirements for the use, care, and protection of abrasive wheels); the wheel blotter and the machine nameplate are the authority.

assumptions.name: Rated speed governs
assumptions.value: the wheel blotter's rated maximum SFPM and the machine nameplate RPM are the authority

assumptions.name: Fresh wheel
assumptions.value: the full (unworn) wheel diameter is the governing case; a worn wheel turns slower in SFPM

toggle-mechanism-force.formula: F_out = F_in / (2 tan theta), theta the angle of each link from the straight (lockup) line; output travel per unit input travel = 2 tan theta; MA = 1/(2 tan theta).
toggle-mechanism-force.edition: The symmetric toggle-linkage mechanical advantage F_out = F_in/(2 tan theta) (Machinery's Handbook; standard statics of the toggle joint), by name.
toggle-mechanism-force.freeAccess: The toggle-joint force relation is a standard published statics result; the input force and toggle angle are the user's inputs.
toggle-mechanism-force.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
toggle-mechanism-force.editionNote: Mechanical advantage of a symmetric toggle linkage - the mechanism in a hold-down clamp, a knee (toggle) press, a rivet or crimp squeezer, or an injection-mold clamp. Two equal links meet at a knee driven perpendicular to the output line; each link sits at an angle theta from the straight (lockup) line, and F_out = F_in/(2 tan theta). Near lockup (theta small) the advantage diverges - a light hand force becomes a large clamp force, why a toggle clamp snaps hard and holds at over-center - but the output moves only 2 tan theta per unit of input travel (huge force, almost no stroke), and pushing PAST lockup releases the clamp. Ideal frictionless linkage; joint friction, link buckling, pin shear, and the over-center holding geometry are separate. A design aid; Machinery's Handbook and the clamp maker govern.

assumptions.name: Advantage
assumptions.value: F_out = F_in/(2 tan theta) for a symmetric toggle; diverges at lockup (theta -> 0)

assumptions.name: Travel trade-off
assumptions.value: output travel per unit input travel = 2 tan theta = 1/MA; over-travel past lockup releases

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: ideal frictionless linkage; friction, link buckling, pin shear are separate

flatbed-tarp-size.formula: width_needed_ft = load_width + 2 x load_height + 2 x tuck; tarps_needed = ceil((load_length - overlap) / (tarp_length - overlap)); covered_length_ft = tarps x tarp_length - (tarps - 1) x overlap; total_weight_lb = tarps x weight each.
flatbed-tarp-size.edition: Flatbed tarp coverage from the wrap geometry -- width equals the load width plus twice the height plus twice the tuck, because the tarp comes down both sides -- and the shingled-overlap length relation, by name; standard flatbed practice on public geometry. The actual tarps on the truck and the driver's judgment govern.
flatbed-tarp-size.freeAccess: The coverage geometry is public. The load and tarp dimensions, the overlap, and the tuck allowance are the driver's own values.
flatbed-tarp-size.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flatbed-tarp-size.editionNote: The width requirement is the one people get wrong, because a tarp has to come down both sides of the load and not merely across the top. A load eight feet wide standing six feet above the deck needs twenty feet of tarp across before any allowance for tucking under the edge of the load and getting a bungee on it, so the requirement is the load width plus twice the height plus twice the tuck. A tarp sized to the deck width is not a tarp, it is a lid. The length side is a shingling problem rather than a division. Tarps overlap toward the rear so that road wind cannot get under a leading edge, and every overlap costs its own length from the run, so three twenty-foot tarps lapped four feet do not cover sixty feet, they cover fifty-two. The weight line is not a footnote. A steel tarp runs sixty to a hundred pounds, so a three-tarp load is a couple of hundred pounds of payload and, more to the point, a couple of hundred pounds a driver has to get onto a load by hand, which is where tarping injuries come from. When the height requirement passes what a steel tarp can span, the answer is lumber tarps rather than a bigger steel tarp.

assumptions.name: Width comes down both sides
assumptions.value: width = load width + 2 x height + 2 x tuck; a tarp sized to the deck is a lid

assumptions.name: Shingled overlap
assumptions.value: each lap costs its own length from the run; tarps overlap toward the rear so wind cannot get under a leading edge

assumptions.name: Weight is handling
assumptions.value: 60 to 100 lb per steel tarp, lifted by hand onto the load

cipp-liner-thickness.formula: ASTM F1216 X1.1, partially deteriorated: external pressure = 2 K E C / (1 - nu squared) x (1 / (DR - 1)) cubed / N, with the ovality reduction C = ((1 - q) / (1 + q) squared) cubed and Poisson's ratio 0.3; thickness = host diameter / DR.
cipp-liner-thickness.edition: The ASTM F1216 X1.1 groundwater-buckling relation by name, for the partially deteriorated design case only. The fully deteriorated case is a different relation requiring the soil modulus, the live load, and the water buoyancy factor; the cipp-fully-deteriorated tile computes it. For the partially deteriorated case the standard also requires the X1.2 bending check where the host pipe is out of round and holds the dimension ratio to 100 or less, and the design thickness is the greatest of those (Iowa SUDAS 14C-2; NCDOT Pipe Liner Manual) -- this computes X1.1 alone. ASTM F1216, the liner manufacturer's tested properties, and the design engineer govern.
cipp-liner-thickness.freeAccess: The buckling relation is published engineering; the modulus, ovality, and enhancement factor are the user's own measured and manufacturer-supplied values, and no F1216 table is reproduced.
cipp-liner-thickness.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cipp-liner-thickness.editionNote: The two design cases are not variations on a theme. In the partially deteriorated case the host pipe is still structurally sound and the liner's only job is to resist external groundwater pressure trying to buckle it inward, so the thickness comes out modest. In the fully deteriorated case the host is assumed gone and the liner is the pipe, carrying soil load, live load, and groundwater as a standalone structure -- a much thicker section. Choosing the case is an engineering judgment about the host pipe's condition, made from a CCTV survey and the pipe's history rather than from a preference. Two inputs dominate the buckling case. Ovality is the first, and it bites steeply because the reduction factor goes as a cube of a term that falls with out-of-roundness, so a few percent costs real thickness -- and ovality is measured rather than assumed. The second is the modulus, and the trap there is TIME: CIPP creeps, so the fifty-year modulus is roughly half the short-term value, and a design run on the short-term number is unconservative by a large margin. Both are computed here so the penalty is visible rather than argued. Groundwater head is the load, and it is taken at the highest credible level rather than at the level on the day of the survey.

assumptions.name: Ovality goes as a cube
assumptions.value: a few percent of out-of-roundness is real thickness, and it is measured not assumed

assumptions.name: Use the LONG-TERM modulus
assumptions.value: creep halves it over fifty years, and the short-term number is unconservative

assumptions.name: The fully deteriorated case is a different relation
assumptions.value: it needs the soil modulus, live load, and buoyancy factor; cipp-fully-deteriorated computes it

steel-web-local-strength.formula: WLY Rn = Fy tw (5k + lb) interior, Fy tw (2.5k + lb) end (Omega 1.50 / phi 1.00); WC Rn = 0.80 tw^2 [1 + 3(lb/d)(tw/tf)^1.5] sqrt(E Fy tf/tw) interior; within d/2 of the end WC Rn = 0.40 tw^2 [1 + 3(lb/d)(tw/tf)^1.5] sqrt(E Fy tf/tw), with [1 + (4 lb/d - 0.2)(tw/tf)^1.5] when lb/d > 0.2 (Omega 2.00 / phi 0.75); governing = min of the factored pair. (E = 29,000 ksi)
steel-web-local-strength.edition: The AISC 360-22 J10.2 web local yielding and J10.3 web crippling limit states under a concentrated transverse force, with the interior/end coefficients and their differing resistance/safety factors, by name.
steel-web-local-strength.freeAccess: AISC 360 is free to read at aisc.org (Specification for Structural Steel Buildings); the J10 provisions are in the published specification.
steel-web-local-strength.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
steel-web-local-strength.editionNote: The AISC 360-22 J10.2 web local yielding Rn = Fy tw (5k + lb) interior / (2.5k + lb) end (phi = 1.00 / Omega = 1.50) and J10.3 web crippling Rn = 0.80 tw^2 [1 + 3(lb/d)(tw/tf)^1.5] sqrt(E Fy tf/tw) interior (phi = 0.75 / Omega = 2.00), E = 29,000 ksi, k = kdes. This returns the two web limit states under a concentrated transverse force at an interior or near-end location - it uses the interior/end forms as selected, including the 0.40 end coefficient (Eq. J10-5a) and the (4 lb/d - 0.2) bracket when lb/d > 0.2 (Eq. J10-5b) within d/2 of the end, and does not cover web sidesway or compression buckling (J10.4/J10.5), or the bearing-stiffener design itself. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Web local yielding
assumptions.value: Fy tw (5k + lb) interior; (2.5k + lb) within a member depth of the end

assumptions.name: Web crippling
assumptions.value: 0.80 tw^2 [1 + 3(lb/d)(tw/tf)^1.5] sqrt(E Fy tf/tw) for an interior force

assumptions.name: Differing factors
assumptions.value: Omega 1.50 vs 2.00 (phi 1.00 vs 0.75) - the governing limit state can flip between ASD and LRFD

steel-beam-ltb.formula: Mp = Fy Zx; Lp = 1.76 ry sqrt(E/Fy); Lr per AISC Eq. F2-6 (c = 1); Lb <= Lp: Mn = Mp; Lp < Lb <= Lr: Mn = Cb[Mp - (Mp - 0.7 Fy Sx)(Lb - Lp)/(Lr - Lp)] <= Mp; Lb > Lr: Fcr = Cb pi^2 E/(Lb/rts)^2 sqrt(1 + 0.078 Jc/(Sx ho)(Lb/rts)^2), Mn = Fcr Sx <= Mp. ASD = Mn/1.67; LRFD = 0.90 Mn. (E = 29,000 ksi)
steel-beam-ltb.edition: The AISC 360-22 Section F2 lateral-torsional buckling provisions for a doubly-symmetric compact I-shape bending about its strong axis (Lp, the Eq. F2-6 Lr, the linear inelastic branch, and the Eq. F2-4 elastic critical stress with c = 1), by name; E = 29,000 ksi and the Omega_b = 1.67 / phi_b = 0.90 factors are named constants.
steel-beam-ltb.freeAccess: AISC 360 is free to read at aisc.org (Specification for Structural Steel Buildings); the shape properties are in the AISC Steel Construction Manual tables.
steel-beam-ltb.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
steel-beam-ltb.editionNote: The AISC 360-22 Section F2 limits Lp = 1.76 ry sqrt(E/Fy) and Lr (Eq. F2-6, computed with c = 1), the inelastic Mn = Cb[Mp - (Mp - 0.7 Fy Sx)(Lb - Lp)/(Lr - Lp)] <= Mp, and the elastic Fcr = Cb pi^2 E/(Lb/rts)^2 sqrt(1 + 0.078 (Jc/(Sx ho))(Lb/rts)^2), with E = 29,000 ksi. This covers doubly-symmetric compact I-shapes bending about the strong axis (the F2 case) - it does not cover noncompact or slender flanges/webs (F3-F5) or channels and singly-symmetric shapes, and it assumes the entered Cb matches the moment diagram (1.0 is conservative). A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Bracing limits
assumptions.value: Lp = 1.76 ry sqrt(E/Fy); Lr from the Eq. F2-6 closed form with c = 1 for a doubly-symmetric shape

assumptions.name: Three zones
assumptions.value: full Mp below Lp, linear interpolation to 0.7 Fy Sx at Lr, elastic Fcr Sx beyond, all capped at Mp and scaled by Cb

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: compact doubly-symmetric I-shapes about the strong axis; section properties from the AISC Manual

lateral-earth-pressure.formula: Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2) = (1 - sin phi) / (1 + sin phi); Kp = 1/Ka; Pa = 0.5 Ka gamma H^2 at H/3, plus surcharge Ka q H at H/2; Pp = 0.5 Kp gamma H^2.
lateral-earth-pressure.edition: Rankine (1857) lateral earth pressure, as compiled in Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, and NAVFAC DM-7.02 (Foundations and Earth Structures), by name.
lateral-earth-pressure.freeAccess: NAVFAC DM-7.02 is a free public US Navy design manual; the Rankine coefficient arithmetic is public and printed in every soil-mechanics text.
lateral-earth-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
lateral-earth-pressure.editionNote: Rankine (1857) lateral earth pressure - Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2) = (1 - sin phi)/(1 + sin phi), Kp = 1/Ka = tan^2(45 + phi/2), resultant Pa = 0.5 Ka gamma H^2 at H/3 plus a uniform-surcharge term Ka q H at H/2 - as compiled in Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, and NAVFAC DM-7.02 (Foundations and Earth Structures). gamma defaults to 120 pcf, q to 0. The Rankine case only: a cohesionless soil (the 2c sqrt(Ka) tension-crack reduction of a cohesive backfill is not applied), a vertical wall face with no wall friction (Coulomb theory is required for an inclined or rough face and gives a lower active thrust), a dry level backfill with no water table (a submerged zone must be run with buoyant unit weight plus a separate hydrostatic pressure), and the fully-mobilized active and passive limit states (the wall must move enough to reach them). Take phi and gamma from the geotechnical report. A design aid, not a substitute for a geotechnical engineer's report - the geotechnical engineer of record's recommendation governs.

assumptions.name: Rankine conditions
assumptions.value: cohesionless backfill, vertical frictionless wall face, level dry backfill; Coulomb / cohesive / submerged / sloped cases need their own analysis

assumptions.name: Limit states mobilized
assumptions.value: active and passive values require enough wall movement to mobilize them; a braced non-yielding wall sees the higher at-rest K0 = 1 - sin phi

assumptions.name: Passive used cautiously
assumptions.value: the passive thrust is an upper bound needing large movement to develop; designs commonly reduce or neglect it

radiator-edr-output.formula: heat_output_btu_hr = edr_sqft x system_k (k = 240 steam, 150 hot water); gross_boiler_btu_hr = heat_output_btu_hr x (1 + pickup_factor). I=B=R pickup ~0.33 steam, ~0.15 hot water.
radiator-edr-output.edition: Equivalent Direct Radiation (EDR) heat-output conversion (Hydronics Institute / I=B=R basis), by name; the radiator EDR from the maker or a measurement, the actual piping and pickup, and the boiler's I=B=R net rating govern.
radiator-edr-output.freeAccess: The EDR constants (240 BTU/hr per sq ft steam, 150 hot water) and the pounds-formula-style gross-up are public heating practice; the connected EDR and the pickup allowance are the job's values.
radiator-edr-output.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
radiator-edr-output.editionNote: Old steam and hot-water heating systems rate their cast-iron radiators and convectors in EDR, Equivalent Direct Radiation, measured in square feet, and converting that rating to a heat output in BTU per hour uses a fixed constant that depends only on the system type. One square foot of EDR emits 240 BTU per hour on a STEAM system -- the Hydronics Institute / I=B=R basis, defined for one square foot radiating with 215 F steam inside and a 70 F room -- and 150 BTU per hour on a HOT-WATER system, defined at a 170 F average water temperature in a 70 F room. So six radiators totaling 320 square feet of EDR deliver 320 times 240, or 76,800 BTU per hour on steam, and the same 320 square feet would deliver 320 times 150, or 48,000 BTU per hour if piped for hot water. This tile works in the direction a fitter actually uses when replacing a boiler: add up the EDR of the radiators already in the building, convert to the connected heat load, and then size the boiler. Boiler sizing adds a pickup allowance -- extra output to warm the cold distribution piping and the mass of iron on a cold morning start -- so the gross boiler output is the connected load times one plus the pickup fraction, the I=B=R pickup being about 0.33 (33%) for steam and about 0.15 for hot water. The 76,800 BTU per hour steam load therefore calls for a boiler with a gross output near 102,000 BTU per hour, which is selected by matching its published NET steam rating (in square feet of EDR or BTU per hour) to the connected load. This is the counting-radiators direction; the companion boiler-horsepower tile converts a boiler's nameplate rating the other way. It is a sizing aid; the actual radiator EDR from the manufacturer's data or a physical measurement, the real piping runs and their pickup, and the boiler's I=B=R net rating govern the final selection.

assumptions.name: EDR constants
assumptions.value: 1 sq ft EDR = 240 BTU/hr steam (215 F / 70 F room), 150 BTU/hr hot water (170 F avg / 70 F room)

assumptions.name: Boiler pickup
assumptions.value: gross = net x (1 + pickup); I=B=R pickup ~0.33 steam, ~0.15 hot water; select by the boiler's NET rating

capacitor-bank-voltage-rise.formula: percent rise = bank kVAR x reactance from the source to the bank / (10 x line-to-line kV squared); rise in volts on a 120 V base = percent rise x 1.2; leading current = kVAR / (sqrt(3) x kV); the largest fixed bank is the relation worked backwards against the headroom at light load.
capacitor-bank-voltage-rise.edition: The distribution capacitor voltage-rise relation as standard practice, by name, with ANSI C84.1 Range A named for the limit the result is tested against. The limit and both pre-switching voltages are entered because the adopted range and the feeder's profile are local. ANSI C84.1, IEEE 1036, the utility's capacitor application guide, and a distribution power-flow study govern.
capacitor-bank-voltage-rise.freeAccess: One multiplication and one division; no ANSI voltage table is reproduced, the limit is entered.
capacitor-bank-voltage-rise.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
capacitor-bank-voltage-rise.editionNote: A capacitor injects leading reactive current, and that current flowing back through the reactance between the bank and the source raises the voltage at the point of connection. The further out the bank sits the bigger its voltage effect and the smaller its loss-reduction effect per kVAR, so the two goals pull in opposite directions. The case that binds is light load: a fixed bank sized for peak-load power factor is still connected at three in the morning, when the drop it was cancelling is gone and the rise it produces is the whole story. That is why the result is reported at both conditions and why the largest bank that still fits under the limit at light load is worked out rather than argued.

assumptions.name: Steady state, one bank, radial feeder
assumptions.value: no switching transient, inrush, or restrike

assumptions.name: The voltage limit is entered
assumptions.value: the adopted ANSI C84.1 range is local

assumptions.name: No harmonic resonance check
assumptions.value: that is a separate screen and the other way a bank sizing fails

deadband-cycling-rate.formula: load = UA x (setpoint - outdoor); on = C x deadband / (Q - load); off = C x deadband / load; cycles per hour = load (Q - load) / (C x deadband x Q); duty = load / Q; the maximum is Q / (4 C x deadband), at 50% duty.
deadband-cycling-rate.edition: A first-order two-position cycling model: one thermal capacitance, one loss coefficient, and a fixed-output device. Not a simulation.
deadband-cycling-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
deadband-cycling-rate.editionNote: DEADBAND AND CYCLING ARE INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL -- halving the band exactly doubles the starts -- while THE DUTY CYCLE DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE DEADBAND AT ALL. A narrow band does not make equipment run more, it makes it START more, which is the damaging thing. OVERSIZING WORKS THROUGH THE MAXIMUM: the peak rate scales directly with capacity, so doubling the equipment doubles the worst case (3.12 to 6.25 per hour on the worked case). AND THE PEAK MOVES TO A COLDER DAY, NOT A MILDER ONE -- the oversized unit reaches 50% duty at 20 degF against the right-sized unit's 45 -- which inverts the usual folklore. The stronger statement the arithmetic supports is that an oversized unit cycles more at EVERY load: cycles = (load / C x deadband) x (1 - load / Q) is strictly increasing in Q. Anti-short-cycle timers decouple the real machine from this relation entirely, and modulating or staged equipment does not cycle this way at all.

assumptions.name: First-order space
assumptions.value: one capacitance, one UA; internal mass, gains and infiltration are not modelled
assumptions.source: a teaching model, not a simulation

assumptions.name: Instantaneous equipment
assumptions.value: no start-up transient, purge, pull-down or minimum off timer

assumptions.name: Two-position control only
assumptions.value: modulating, staged and variable-speed equipment do not cycle this way

pon-split-loss-budget.formula: splitter loss = 10 log10(N) + excess; remaining fiber budget = class budget - splitter - connectors - splices - margin; reach = remaining/attenuation.
pon-split-loss-budget.edition: Logarithmic split loss and an entered PON optical-class budget. Class limits and component losses are not bundled.
pon-split-loss-budget.freeAccess: A logarithm and additive dB budget.
pon-split-loss-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pon-split-loss-budget.editionNote: THE SPLITTER SPENDS MOST OF THE BUDGET. In the worked class B+ example, a 1:32 splitter with excess loss consumes 17.55 dB of 28 dB and leaves 7.85 dB for fiber, or 22.4 km at 0.35 dB/km. Doubling to 1:64 adds exactly 3.01 dB and cuts that reach to 13.8 km.

assumptions.name: Worst wavelength entered
assumptions.value: the path must close upstream and downstream

assumptions.name: Uniform component losses
assumptions.value: splitter excess and connector/splice loss are entered

assumptions.name: Maximum-loss side only
assumptions.value: minimum path loss and receiver overload are not checked

carbonation-volumes-pressure.formula: volumes = (psig + 14.695) x k(T) - 0.003342, with k(T) = 0.01821 + 0.09011 e^(-(T - 32) / 43.11), T in degF; solved both ways.
carbonation-volumes-pressure.edition: A fit to the published CO2 solubility tables at sea level. The brewery's own dissolved-CO2 measurement governs.
carbonation-volumes-pressure.freeAccess: The solubility tables are published openly.
carbonation-volumes-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
carbonation-volumes-pressure.editionNote: The temperature term dominates: a cooler a few degrees warm flattens the beer with the gauge unmoved, and chasing it with pressure over-carbonates once the cooler is fixed.

assumptions.name: Altitude
assumptions.value: sea-level atmosphere; altitude lowers it

assumptions.name: Range
assumptions.value: 28 to 80 degF

collection-vehicle-payload.formula: in-body density = loose density x compaction ratio; body payload = body volume x that density; chassis payload = gross vehicle weight rating - tare weight; the smaller governs, and the legal fill = chassis payload / in-body density.
collection-vehicle-payload.edition: Manufacturer ratings against the applicable weight law. Axle-by-axle loading, not just gross weight, is what an enforcement scale checks.
collection-vehicle-payload.freeAccess: Public arithmetic; the ratings come from the chassis and body manufacturers.
collection-vehicle-payload.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
collection-vehicle-payload.editionNote: When the chassis governs there is no gauge and no warning -- a crew filling to the pack panel is simply over the rating on the road. Specify the chassis and body together so the BODY governs and the judgement leaves the crew.

assumptions.name: Axle loading
assumptions.value: not computed here; gross weight alone does not establish legality

assumptions.name: Loose density
assumptions.value: moves with the weather, so the legal fill moves with it too

hurricane-debris-estimate.formula: Q (cy) = H x C x V x B x S, with H = population / persons per household (3, carried unrounded); C = 2, 8, 26, 50, 80 cy per household for categories 1 to 5; V = 1.1, 1.3, 1.5; B = 1.0, 1.2, 1.3; S = 1.0 or 1.3; band Q x 0.7 to Q x 1.3; woody = Q x woody fraction, C&D = the rest, split 42% burnable, 5% soil, 15% metals, 38% landfill; tons = cy / (softwood 6, hardwood 4, mixed 4, C&D 2).
hurricane-debris-estimate.edition: FEMA-325, Public Assistance Debris Management Guide (July 2007), Appendix B, USACE Hurricane Debris Estimating Model, Step 1 and its stated plus-or-minus 30% accuracy, with the Hurricane Andrew composition and C&D split from the same guide; volume-to-weight factors as restated in FEMA 329, Debris Estimating Field Guide (September 2010). FEMA-325 is superseded in part by the Public Assistance Program and Policy Guide; the model's factors remain the published USACE values.
hurricane-debris-estimate.freeAccess: FEMA-325 and FEMA 329 are free federal publications on fema.gov; every factor is a public-domain USACE or FEMA figure.
hurricane-debris-estimate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hurricane-debris-estimate.editionNote: The model is a household count times a per-household debris factor for the storm category, adjusted for trees, commercial buildings, and rain. The category factor carries most of the spread and the multipliers can add about 150% on top; the stated accuracy is 30% either way, so the band is the answer and the single figure is its middle. The guide's Harrison County example carries the household count unrounded, which is why it prints 6,992,374 rather than the 6,992,417 a rounded count gives. The composition split decides the disposal plan, and the guide's default is from one storm; another produced the reverse, so the woody fraction is an input to revisit once the first loads are seen. The model describes the wet-storm increase for category 3 and above, and the tile flags a wet multiplier on a weaker storm. It was built for hurricanes, not tornado, flood, earthquake, or wildfire debris.

assumptions.name: Three persons per household
assumptions.value: the model's household count is population / 3 unless a local figure is entered

assumptions.name: Plus or minus 30%
assumptions.value: a planning forecast, replaced by field estimates and load tickets as they come in

assumptions.name: Conversion factors are defaults
assumptions.value: C&D 2 cy per ton, hardwood and mixed 4, softwood 6; field tests may be needed to confirm them
